ALLEGED DENIAL OF PRESS
speechtext:
I wish to raise a question of privilege arising out of the fact that Mr. Raymond Rodgers, correspondent for the St. Catharines Standard, has been expelled from the press gallery. I should like to attempt to establish a prima facie case of privilege based on one reason or a combination of several reasons, following which, if permission is granted, I am prepared to move a substantive motion which would take care of the matter.
First I should like to quote to Your Honour from Beauchesne, citation 103, paragraph 2 which says "the house has always asserted the right to provide for the constitution of its own body, the right to regulate its own proceedings, and the right to enforce its privileges." Again Beauchesne, citation 107, reads as follows:
Whatever matter arises concerning either house of parliament ought to be discussed and adjudged in that house to which it relates, and not elsewhere.
I contend that matters affecting the internal economy of the house are questions of privilege. There is, of course, public expenditure for the press gallery of the house, payment for which is provided through the internal economy commission. The amount is something like $100,000 annually.
The second point is that an exception has been made respecting the administration of the galleries, including both the press gallery and the diplomatic gallery. This exception has not been concurred in by the house.
The third point is that I think you will agree a legitimate breach of privilege can be established in the matter of time, that is to say that the matter of time is urgent.
Motions affecting the internal economy of the house, as I pointed out, are questions of privilege affecting the privileges of all members collectively and may always be considered in the house without the notice necessary in the case of motions generally. This is pointed out in standing order 17, and Bourinot's Parliamentary Procedure and Practice on pages 375 and 376, where a case
is cited concerning the translation of the official debates which is reported in the debates of 1876.
The present matter relates to the principle by which persons are accredited to the press gallery, and the application of that principle to the credentials of a particular correspondent. The house in the past has delegated to the Speaker the enunciation of a principle and the application of that principle to particular cases. Over the years since that delegation of authority, however, we have perhaps lost sight of the fact that what is involved is the fundamental privilege of each and every member of the house to object to strangers in the galleries, according to standing order 13. Therefore each and every member is responsible for and must consent to any rule made by way of an exception to that privilege.
As well, we are also responsible for the application of that rule in this particular case. Each member's responsibility is even heavier in respect of the exception that has been made because due to the lack of space and facilities for the press gallery the exception is a discriminatory one that admits certain correspondents and excludes others. As you well know, Mr. Speaker, the present difficulty has continued over several sessions and continues each sitting day of the house, so that the question of privilege is one that renews itself with each sitting and is immediately before the house on the occasion of each sitting.
On October 29 last, Mr. Speaker, you advised the house that the question of principle and the question of the individual case were of deep concern to you but that due to the pressure of other urgent matters it was physically impossible for you to determine the matter shortly. There can be no doubt that the effect of the unavoidable delay in the particular instance of this individual has had the result of deciding the matter during the interim before a determination of the principle, in favour of one of the parties against the other. This decision, founded only in delay, may ultimately be the correct one according to the justice of the case, or it may not be.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, if I am granted a prima facie case of privilege I am prepared to move, seconded by the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. McNulty):

Denial of Press Gallery Privileges
That the Sergeant-at-Arms, pursuant to standing order 88, be instructed to grant pro tem a card admitting Raymond Rodgers to the press galleries of this house.
I have a large number of other citations with me this afternoon which I could quote to you, Mr. Speaker, but I do not particularly wish to take up the time of the house. However, in my view these precedents will establish that there is an injustice by reason of delay. There has been a transfer of the administrative responsibility of this house to a body outside of the house who are not, in turn, responsible to us. Therefore, on this basis, I would implore that you grant a prima facie case of privilege so that I can move a substantive motion to clear up the matter.

Well, recent experience may have shown it is somewhat dangerous to allow too much discussion on a point of privilege, because privilege is an extraordinary proceeding and should be stated as briefly as possible. Nevertheless, I think the discussion this afternoon illustrates the fact that this is more in the nature of a complaint than a privilege, but before reaching that conclusion may I be permitted to call the attention of hon. members to citation 104(5) in Beauchesne:
As a motion taken at the time for matters of privilege is thereby given precedence over the prearranged program of public business, the Speaker requires to be satisfied, both that there is a prima facie case that a breach of privilege has been committed, and also that the matter is being raised at the earliest opportunity. If he is not so satisfied he may allow the member to make a statement with a view to ascertaining whether or not a prima facie case can be made out.
Of course that was the reason for listening carefully to the hon. member for Medicine Hat. Further, citation 113 in Beauchesne reads in part:
Members often raise so-called "questions of privilege" on matters which should be dealt with as personal explanations or corrections, either in the debates or the proceedings of the house. A question of privilege ought rarely to come up in parliament. It should be dealt with by a motion giving the house power to impose a reparation or to apply a remedy.
Of course it is my duty to arrive at a conclusion as to whether a prima facie case of breach of privilege of the house has been made out. Also, a question of privilege is a question relating to the rights and privileges of the house as a whole, or of its members individually, and to the conduct and honour of such members. What is submitted to the house today seems to be more in the nature of a complaint, criticism or grievance concerning the internal economy and administration of the house, and in my opinion should be treated as other possible grievances against the internal economy and administration of the house. The rules governing the internal economy commission are set forth in detail in the House of Commons and Senate Act.
Now, inasmuch as this matter has been under consideration for many months, in fact even years, it hardly qualifies as having been raised at the earliest opportunity, but I admit that is a rather slim limb on which to rely. Some time ago I told the house that the matter was still under active consideration, and that is the position today. Therefore I regret to say that the question as raised does not satisfy me as being a prima facie case of a breach of the privilege of the house.

maintopic: STUDIES OF WATER LEVELS, ST. LAWRENCE RIVER
speechtext:
1. The level of water in the St. Lawrence has been under study for several years and the studies will continue. The present low-level cycle is due actually to the small amount of precipitation which has fallen in the drainage basins of the Ottawa river, the great lakes and the St. Lawrence river.
2.	The studies include various suggestions to control the flow of lake Ontario and concerning the effects of the holding up of water in the upper Ottawa, as well as studies on models and on the spot for the future construction of protective works in the St. Lawrence river, at Montreal and downstream from Montreal.
Studies on the control of the flow of lake Ontario come under the international St. Lawrence river board of control, on behalf of the international joint commission; those concerning the Ottawa river drainage basin are undertaken by the federal-provincial Ottawa river board of engineers and those made at Montreal and downstream, mainly by the Department of Transport.
Studies of the factors affecting the water level of lake Ontario and consequently the flow and level of the St. Lawrence river have also been made by the international lake Ontario board of engineers, on behalf of the joint international commission, from 1952 to 1958.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION IN CANADA OF SUBMARINES FOR CANADIAN NAVY

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION IN CANADA OF SUBMARINES FOR CANADIAN NAVY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Acting Prime Minister. In view of the fact that cancellation of the frigate program will result in the laying off of up to 10,000 Canadians in the shipbuilding and related industries, will the government reconsider its decision to purchase three submarines outside of Canada and launch its own submarine building program in our country, as this type of warship can be built efficiently by our Canadian shipyards?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSTRUCTION IN CANADA OF SUBMARINES FOR CANADIAN NAVY
speechtext:
I am grateful to the hon. member for having given notice to the Prime Minister's office that he intended to ask this question. I presume that it is based on a purported statement by the president of Davie Shipbuilding Limited appearing in this morning's 
Gazette, and which would appear to be an estimate on the part of the individual quoted as to the number of personnel who might have been employed if the general purpose frigate program had been continued.
It is a fact, however, that Canadian shipyards will get substantial benefit from the $110 million shipbuilding program announced by the Minister of Transport and the $50 million program forecast by the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys. The Minister of National Defence has explained to the house the reason for the cancellation of the frigate program. He has explained also to the special committee on defence the reasons for the purchase of the three submarines from the United Kingdom. I have nothing to add to what he has said in this regard.
In so far as a possible submarine construction program in Canada is concerned, the Minister of National Defence also told the defence committee yesterday that we are now undertaking a thorough study of our future naval requirements, and that once those have been determined it will be the policy of the government to undertake production in Canadian yards.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION IN CANADA OF SUBMARINES FOR CANADIAN NAVY
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. Is the minister aware that the programs that have been announced by the Minister of Transport and by the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys were programs that were already drafted under the previous administration, in great part, and that the abandonment of the frigate program and the buying of submarines outside of Canada is going to be a tremendous blow to employment in the shipyards of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSTRUCTION IN CANADA OF SUBMARINES FOR CANADIAN NAVY
speechtext: I thought this was a supplementary question that was being directed to me, but I note now that it is a statement. It is not a fact, let me assure the hon. member, that this program was prepared by the former administration. The former administration had something to do with the 40 per cent aspect of the program-

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION IN CANADA OF SUBMARINES FOR CANADIAN NAVY
speechtext: "Something to do;" that is generous.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSTRUCTION IN CANADA OF SUBMARINES FOR CANADIAN NAVY
speechtext: -but the program announced by my colleagues, the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys is an entirely new program.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION IN CANADA OF SUBMARINES FOR CANADIAN NAVY
speechtext: No, it is not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONSTRUCTION IN CANADA OF SUBMARINES FOR CANADIAN NAVY
speechtext:
These programs, as my two colleagues have indicated, will provide a tremendous amount of employment for the shipyards of the country.

speechtext:
The house in committee on Bill No. C-88, respecting an order of His Excellency the Governor in Council entitled the surcharge on imports order, and to restore certain rates of customs duties and tariff benefits expressed to be withdrawn thereby-Mr. Gordon-Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.
On clause 1.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MEASURE VALIDATING ORDER IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
Because a considerable
amount of time has elapsed since this bill received second reading, hon. members will perhaps expect me to make a short statement at this stage.
The bill has several related purposes. The first is to confirm the surcharge on imports order which was passed by the governor in
4462	HOUSE OF
Measure Validating Order in Council council on June 24, 1962. That order was made on the basis of section 4 of the Customs Tariff and section 22 of the Financial Administration Act. The order provided, in effect, that the general tariff, instead of more favourable tariffs, should apply to certain commodities when imported into Canada but it then went on to remit the duties on such commodities to the extent necessary to bring it about that no duty was, by the first part of the order, increased by more than 15, 10 or 5 per cent, depending upon the commodity.
The second purpose of the bill is to restore, effective April 1, 1963, the more favourable tariff rates above referred to.
The third purpose is to limit the effect of future like orders to a six months period unless during that period any such order is approved by parliament.
I do not wish to keep alive a debate which was somewhat acrimonious and, I think, rather irrelevant, as to the nature of opinions that were given or not given concerning the validity of the surcharge on imports order. In describing the debate as somewhat acrimonious and irrelevant I accept my share of responsibility in the matter. We would do well, I think, to return now to what the Minister of Finance said in announcing that a measure of the nature of Bill C-88 would be introduced. He said that the legality of the order had been challenged and the matter was before the courts; that this posed a difficult problem, because in many cases those who paid the surcharges had passed the amounts on to their customers, and those customers perhaps to their own customers, and so on. He said it would not be possible to unscramble a situation of this kind and that one effect of the proposed legislation would be to prevent any massive attempt at obtaining refund of moneys in fact paid by now unidentifiable Canadians. In addition to this consideration, that the people who recovered the money might not be those actually entitled to it, there is the other very important consideration that the country has budgeted on the basis of this money, and we need it.
That this bill is, in the circumstances, at least a wise precautionary matter, I am sure the majority of the house will agree. That the fear of the government is not illusory is borne out by the fact that there are already pending in the exchequer court actions for the recovery of many million dollars, with more to be expected should these succeed.

subtopic: MEASURE VALIDATING ORDER IN COUNCIL
speechtext: How many actions have been brought?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MEASURE VALIDATING ORDER IN COUNCIL
speechtext:
I think I can give that figure. There are approximately ten at the moment. These actions were taken, these suits were brought, by serious and competent counsel [Mr. Chevrier.l

who do not lightly lead their clients into litigation of this nature.
As to opinions, I only want to say this: When the order was first passed there was an oral opinion, and having regard to the urgency with which the matter was regarded by the then government, it is perhaps not surprising that that was so. But oral opinions are illusive things and, in point of conclusiveness, it is difficult to nail them down afterwards. I have no doubt that the government believed that, after the discussion between the Departments of Finance and Justice in the course of which the oral opinion was expressed, they were warranted in assuming the risk, or they may even have been convinced there was no risk. I have made it clear that I do not share that view but I readily concede that the government acted upon it. As to a written opinion, I can only repeat that there is absolutely nothing upon the files of the Department of Justice. I understand that the deputy minister did give the former minister of justice some material to use in debate quite some time after the order was passed. This is common practice. The nature and contents of that communication, however, in so far as I am concerned, rest between the deputy minister and the former minister of justice in the same way that I hope confidential communications between myself and the deputy minister will still rest between us, after I have left this office. I have not seen it and have not inquired into it because I would regard it as confidential and not subject to disclosure to a new administration. Whatever the communication was, it is obvious that it was confidential material prepared for the minister in a debate on a politically controversial matter and was never considered as material that should be retained upon a file.
In summation we say that, at the least, there are doubts about the validity of the order and these doubts compel that so important a matter should now be put at rest by this bill.
If I may, I should like to ask my colleague the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to move:
That in clause 1 of C-88 the word "validly" in line 9 be deleted.

Certainly the amendment which has just been moved to clause 1 will not be opposed by this side, because I have precisely the same proposal in draft form on my desk. In fact, I intended to move a similar amendment myself later this afternoon.
I suppose that since the experience of Saul of Tarsus on the road to Damascus we have

not seen a greater conversion than has been evident on the part of the hon. gentleman today. We know that Saul kicked against the pricks and that he saw a great light. I am not sure whether the Minister of Justice has seen a great light or whether it was the pricks, in his case, which led to his conversion, but I agree with him that this has been a subject of acrimonious discussion and that there would be no purpose served in reviving it at this time. I must say, however, that the acrimony was not engendered from this side of the house, or rather from the side on which we then sat but, rather, that it was produced by the various members who criticized our action on that occasion.
I shall not go into the subject at great length this afternoon. As the minister has said, this action was taken at the time of an exchange crisis. The government acted with decision and authority. Undoubtedly, it acted under some degree of pressure. Whether or not there were opinions at that time, written or oral-the minister says, now, there was an oral opinion and, obviously, no government would have taken action of that kind until it had received an opinion which approved thereof-is not at this point a matter of primary concern. But since this is, I assume, the last occasion on which this matter will be discussed in the house, I will refer to a statement made by my former colleague who preceded me as minister of finance, the Hon. Donald Fleming. In referring to this matter- and the reference will be found on page 291 of Hansard of October 9, 1962-he had this to say in connection with the validity of this order:
My first point is that we have proceeded on the advice of the law officers of the crown in the proper manner-

He was minister of justice; that is correct. Let me continue the quotation.
-and the advice we have is that the measures which were introduced by orders in council in June, which took effect one minute after midnight on June 25, are proper and legal; that the government had full power to proceed to pass those orders in council, and that those powers so exercised were conferred upon the governor in council by parliament. There can be no question about the validity of those orders in council.
That was a statement by the then minister of justice who had been minister of finance at the time the orders were passed. During all the various questions of privilege that were raised and the discussion of the motion to produce the documents put forward by the hon. member for Essex East, now Secretary of State for External Affairs, I never heard anyone suggest that this action which was taken in the interests of Canada was not good
Measure Validating Order in Council and proper. The only questions I have heard raised are (a) whether it was done on the advice of the law officers of the crown and, (b) whether it was done under the authority of an act of parliament.
Some reference has been made, of course, to the action taken by a preceding government in 1947 and the fact that that government afterwards brought in legislation to validate the action it had taken. I suggest there is no analogy whatsoever between the action of the government in 1947 and the action which was taken by the government of which I had the honour to be a member, in connection with the so called surcharge order.
What happened in 1947 was a very crude and wrong thing from the standpoint of strict legality. One night in October a voice came on the air. Undoubtedly the voice was that of the then minister of finance, the Hon. Douglas Abbott, although there was no proof and no identification whatsoever. This voice then proceeded to say: As of midnight tonight we are increasing the excise taxes by X per cent. Bang, that was it. Without any authority of parliament the act was changed over the radio. This voice said: Taxes from here on are going to be Y per cent instead of X per cent as authorized by the statute.
That was in October. The following March a bill was brought into parliament to validate that action. I have the dates here, although I do not know that they are too important. The validating legislation was brought into the house on March 28, I believe, to validate something which had been done six months before. The bill said, of course, that these taxes were to be retroactive to the date when this voice came over the radio.
It has been argued that this is similar to a budget speech in that when the minister of finance brings in his budget he says that certain taxes are going to be imposed and they become effective as of that night. I suggest that there is no analogy whatsoever between the two situations. A budget speech is brought in on a message from His Excellency the Governor General. This is followed by the resolutions. Then there is a motion to go into supply. Finally there is a motion to go into ways and means. Very properly there are many complicated and technical mechanisms whereby parliament safeguards the right to increase taxation.
I am not suggesting that what was done in 1947 was not necessary at that time. I am not criticizing the action that was taken, but I do say it had no reference or relevance whatsoever to the action taken by the government of the present Leader of the Opposition and by the then minister of finance. We acted on the advice of the law officers of the crown,

Measure Validating Order in Council that we were proceeding in accordance with two statutes which had been passed by parliament, one, the Customs Tariff Act, and the other the Financial Administration Act.
There can be no analogy whatsoever between the action taken under those statutes and the action taken back in 1947, possibly because of an emergency. As I said, I am not questioning the advisability of that action at all. However, there is no question whatsoever of any analogy. The fact is that it was certainly necessary for parliament to validate that action because it resulted in a substantial increase in taxation over and above the rates prevailing, and there was no provision whatsoever for doing so in the taxation statutes. Obviously that action had to be validated by statute. It was done posthumously, six months later, and made retroactive to the night when the radio speech had been made.
Some misapprehension and discussion may have been caused in the present instance by the question of whether there was or was not an opinion. A motion was made by the hon. member for Essex East that the opinion, if there was an opinion, be produced. The minister and the government of that day took the position, and I am sure it is one which would be concurred in by the present Minister of Justice, that it would be improper to produce an opinion from an officer of the crown to his minister because, once you start producing such documents, the whole doctrine of confidentiality breaks down and it would be impossible for ministers to obtain the frank and confidential advice of their officers, and vice-versa.
There are precedents which have been exercised by ministers heretofore in such circumstances. I can think of at least two. When the Hon. Mr. Guthrie was minister of justice in the government of Lord Bennett, as he later was, he was asked to produce an opinion in the House of Commons. He refused to do so but he did obtain a letter from the deputy minister of justice, which he read in parliament. It was not the official opinion which he had obtained some time before but a letter which was given the minister for the purposes of parliament. There may be some argument as to what the technical difference may be between the two. In the one case the minister says that the opinion is confidential and he refuses to produce it. In the other case the minister says that parliament demands it and it is in the public interest for parliament to be informed. That is one precedent.
There is another one nearer to home so far as my hon. friends are concerned. When the right hon. Mr. Ilsley, now chief justice of Nova Scotia, was minister of justice-I might say in passing that he is a former member for
[Mr. Nowlan.l
Digby-Annapolis-Kings-he also produced a letter from a deputy minister advising of action which he had taken, not giving the opinion itself but giving a summary and stating the opinion of the law officer that the action was valid.
You will remember, Mr. Chairman, that the hon. member for Essex East moved for the production of this opinion. A debate arose thereon on orders of the day, and the debate was not terminated. Before it could be, some other things happened. But the minister of justice at that time was prepared to produce for parliament a letter from the deputy minister for the information of parliament setting forth his opinion on the action which had been taken by the government of the day with respect to surcharges. I have here the opinion of the deputy minister addressed to the then minister of justice with respect to the surcharge on imports order. If the debate at that time had been continued this opinion would have been produced, and since a question has been raised whether or not an opinion was obtained from Department of Justice I want to put it on the record now for the information of parliament. It is dated November 16, 1962, is addressed to the then minister of justice and says:
You have asked me to furnish you, for the information of parliament, with a statement of my views on the validity of the surcharge on imports order, P.C. 1962-902 of June 24, 1962.
Section 4 of the Customs Tariff, R.S.C. 1952, chapter 60, empowers the governor in council by order to withdraw rates of customs duties more favourable than the general tariff, and to withdraw the benefit of any tariff more favourable than the general tariff. These powers are unrestricted, and oPFonf rvf thfnr pvproise is to produce an increase in tariff rates.
Section 22 of the Financial Administration Act, R.S.C. 1952, chapter 116, empowers the governor in council, on the recommendation of the treasury board whenever he considers it in the public interest, to remit any tax, fee or penalty. The section defines a tax as including any tax, impost, duty or toll payable to Her Majesty, imposed or authorized to be imposed by any act of parliament and provides, inter alia, that a remission thereof pursuant to that section may be total or partial, and may be granted in any particular case or class of case and before the liability therefor arises.
1 am of the opinion that section 1 of the surcharge on imports order withdraws rates and benefits as authorized by the Customs Tariff, and that section 2 partially remits the resultant tax increases as authorized by the Financial Administration Act. In my view, therefore, the surcharge on imports order is a valid exercise of the powers conferred on the governor in council by these two statutes.
This is signed by Elmer A. Driedger, deputy attorney general, and I want to table this document at this time. So far as the record is concerned, I suggest that clears up any doubt. We are not referring now to any opinion which may have been given previously. That is not mentioned in the letter. This is a letter which was produced some

time later, it is true, for the benefit of the House of Commons, and due to circumstances over which we had no great control it was not produced. I wanted to do so at this time.
I do not think there is very much more one can say at this time. I can appreciate the Minister of Justice feeling, on the advice of his officers, that this legislation will facilitate the operation of the government and the department in dealing with litigation. He says that is one reason why he brought in the bill. We are not going to debate that at this time.
I do want to state very emphatically again that in our opinion what we did was based on the statutes of the country, was authorized by parliament and was not only legal but also entirely proper in every way, shape and form and was the proper action to have taken at that time. We have no apologies and no regrets whatever to utter in that connection.
I would have moved certain amendments. I had two, as a matter of fact, which I was going to move because I thought there was an imputation in one section which was unnecessary and unwarranted. I was going to ask this committee to strike these from the record. In view of the statement made by the minister, in view of his action in taking out at least one word which was repugnant to us, the word "validly", I shall not move these amendments. If that word "validly" were allowed to stand there would be the imputation that what we did was invalid, and that certainly could not be accepted by us for a moment.
In view of this action, I do not intend to go further with the amendment. I am glad the minister has taken the position he has. I hope that this will finally clear up this matter, which has been the subject matter of some acrimony and some lengthy discussion. I hope it is clear in the record now that I have said, as my predecessor did before me, that we were acting at all times on the opinion of the law officers of the crown. I hope that the matter will be laid to rest after the passage of this section.

Mr. Chairman, like the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, I have no desire to reactivate the acrimony that surrounded this issue in the last parliament and in the earlier part of this parliament. I hope that I succeed at least as well as the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings did in not raising issues that will reactivate that acrimony. I am not so sure my hon. friend's reference to Mr. Abbott, and his reference now to the question of whether or not there was an opinion last year from the deputy minister of justice, fulfilled the hope expressed by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings.
Even so, Mr. Chairman, before we pass this legislation I think the house has no alternative but to face up to the fact there are a few things that should be said. I was, of course, interested in the suggestion made by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings that in his view there is all the difference in the world between what Mr. Abbott did in 1947 and what the last Conservative government did in 1962. When he proceeded to emphasize the difference, he made quite a point of the fact that in 1947 a voice came on the air, which purported to be the voice of Mr. Abbott. The hon. member said that we had to assume it was his voice. The only comment I wish to make is that science is wonderful. Fifteen years later a voice came on the air again to tell us of certain actions, and the only difference was that in the meantime television had been invented and we not only heard the voice but we saw the face. It was the face of the then prime minister, the present Leader of the Opposition. We recognized his face and we recognized his voice. There was no doubt about it.
However, in both instances we were being advised by the then latest means of communication that the government of the day was imposing certain tax increases. I still think that the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings and his colleagues have a real task on their hands in trying to deal with the proposition that the taxes in 1947 were at least approved by parliament later, whereas the taxes imposed on June 24, 1962, were never approved by parliament, except in so far as they are now before us for retroactive approval.

subtopic: MEASURE VALIDATING ORDER IN COUNCIL
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member if they were not approved by parliament when the statutes were passed some years before?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.

speechtext:
That is the point I am coming to right now. I suggest that the hon. member has indulged in argument by assertion, when he said that the Customs Tariff and Financial Administration Act provided

Measure Validating Order in Council a valid base for the surcharge order in council. If he can argue by assertion, so can I. My reading of these two statutes, particularly my reading of the Financial Administration Act, leads me to believe that the government had a right under the Customs Tariff to make certain changes increasing the rates of tariff, but it had no right under the Financial Administration Act to make the kind of reduction it did, which had the net effect of simply increasing taxes.
It is for this reason the matter is before the courts. The hon. member for Digby-Anna-polis-Kings argues one way and I argue another. He may be a lawyer, while I am not; but I suggest to him the case has been taken before the Exchequer Court of Canada because there is a serious doubt in the minds of very eminent counsel as to the validity of the order in council. We all know how that order in council was composed. In the first place, reliance was placed on the Customs Tariff, where there is authority by order in council to increase the rates of duty by transferring goods from one class of tariff to another. Although that right is in the Customs Tariff, there is no suggestion that the government, by order in council, can arrive at any intermediate rate of tariff. You can move goods from one class to another; in fact, you can make that movement among three different categories. However, there is no suggestion that you can, by order in council, fix some other rate.
In so far as section 22 of the Financial Administration Act is concerned, surely it is quite clear that it is a provision for the remission of taxes or duties or penalties which have been unfairly collected. There is no suggestion that this is a statute that can be used as a basis for cutting down a tax imposed in some other way. Surely, the part of section 22 which requires the publishing in the public accounts of every such remission of more than $1,000 makes it clear that what was envisaged in that section was individual remissions of the kind that have been published from year to year in the public accounts.
Now, my good friend from Digby-Anna-polis-Kings and I could go on arguing this matter as long as we have the right to speak. I do not suppose I could convince him any more than he could convince me. However, there is doubt about the validity of the order in council, and that doubt is confirmed by the fact that the case has been taken to the exchequer court. I think it is unfortunate it has not been possible for the court to make a decision. We have had arguments about it here and in the last parliament. We differed, depending on where we were sitting in the

house. I think it is unfortunate the court has not had a chance to make a decision. One of the by-products of the passage of this legislation will, I suppose, be that the case will disappear from the exchequer court list.
Another very interesting question has arisen here. It arose on August 1 when we had the matter before us. The Minister of Justice told the committee then that the opinion of the deputy minister of justice was that there was some doubt about this order and therefore this legislation should be introduced. We have had it again today. The Minister of Justice tried to play this in a very low key, and I appreciate what he is doing. Still, he told us that there was an oral opinion from the deputy minister of justice to the previous government that this order in council was valid. He told us that he has an opinion from the deputy minister of justice that there is some doubt about it, and that this piece of legislation should be introduced.
This raises some rather serious questions as to the relationship between the government of the day and the Department of Justice. Frequently in this place we are told that such and such is the opinion of justice. It begins to look as though the government of the day gets from justice the opinion it wants. The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings has read into the record a letter from the deputy minister of justice to the then minister of justice, and he gives it now as the authority, presumably, that the government of the day had for believing that this order in council was valid. This letter the hon. member has read to us today was dated November 16, 1962. The order in council was passed on June 24. I listened carefully to that letter, and it does not, unless I missed something, say that Mr. Driedger thought this on June 24. Mr. Driedger was giving to the then minister of justice arguments that he could use in the debate in the House of Commons. He was giving those arguments to the then minister under date of November 16, 1962.
The present Minister of Justice very suavely and very nicely today said these things should not be produced. He was not going to ask for the letters given to the previous minister, and he would not want us to ask for the tabling of his opinion to him. This seemed to soothe the tempers in the house. But the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings has read into the record from a document the present Minister of Justice would not give us. This seems to me to raise a very serious question about the relationship between the government of the day and the Department of Justice, particularly the deputy minister of justice. If these opinions of justice are going to mean any-

Measure Validating Order in Council
thing, if they are going to be valuable to us, surely we have got to get away from a situation where we get one opinion one month and another opinion a few months later.
We are getting these from precisely the same individual, the same person.

I suggest that confidentiality between a minister and his deputy minister should be maintained, but that confidentiality has been destroyed by what has taken place today, and it raises the importance of governments asking from the deputy minister, not opinions that will support what the government happens to want to do, but opinions that are objective and valid all the way down the line.
Mr. Chairman, this underlines what I have said a great many times during various debates on this last session. How much better it would have been if the government of that day had stuck with what it often said it believed in, namely the rights and supremacy of parliament. How much better it would have been if it had brought this matter to parliament.
Parliament was not meeting in June of last year when the crisis was faced and this action taken, by what I think was an invalid order. But I believe even the last parliament, made up of minorities as it was, would have been willing to give approval to the tax changes if parliament had been given a chance to do so and had been given the arguments for them. This is another case that demonstrates the supreme importance of having respect, and holding to that respect, for the rules of the house, for the traditions of parliament, and particularly for the basic principle that the government is at all times responsible to parliament as a whole.
As I say, Mr. Chairman, it seems to us we have no alternative but to support this legislation and to vote for it. If there is doubt about the order in council, then the passing
of this legislation will remove that doubt, at least in so far as the actual collecting of the taxes is concerned. The other thing to do is to leave it to the courts, and if that results in a declaration that the order in council was invalid, then those who have filed their cases in the courts would get their money back. But since they are not the ones who paid it ultimately, since those who did pay it, the consumers, are not identifiable, that would be compounding the injustice that has already developed. Because of that situation we feel we have no alternative but to support the legislation to clean up the doubts and to make sure this situation does not happen again.
In that connection I want to indicate that although the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings has torn up his amendments, I still have one I intend to move when we get to clause 3. May I just say now, while we are on clause 1, that I am glad the government has put clause 3 in the bill, and that it wants to prevent this kind of thing from happening again, or at least to provide some safeguard; but I do not think the government has gone far enough.
I listened carefully to the Minister of Justice. He said one of the purposes of the bill would be that any "future like orders"- although I did not take down all of his words I took down those three-could last only for six months subject to later approval by parliament. That is not going far enough. I do not think there should be any "future like orders". I do not think in the future it should be possible to bring in an order, based in part on the Customs Tariff and in part on the Financial Administration Act, and juggle with the tax rate in the way this was done. Therefore when we come to clause 3 I will move an amendment which seeks to tighten up this legislation a bit more, so as to make sure what happened last year will not happen again.
I stress the point that here we have an example of the importance of paying attention to the letter of the law, paying attention to the principles and practices of our parliamentary democracy, and in particular paying attention to the important principle that governments should not do what they do not have authority to do, and that governments should respect at all times the supremacy and the rights of parliament.

Then he went on to deal with the situation as he sees it, and in the course of his remarks as I heard them, and I paid close attention to them, he cast a reflection on one of our senior civil servants. I have always been of the opinion that this should not be done in the House of Commons, or elsewhere for that matter, because civil servants have not the right of reply. It is all very well in the House of Commons to attack each other, but the great saving feature of the House of Commons is that we have the right of reply.
We do not have the right to reply to accusations made from some other quarters; but I think it is wholly wrong for a member of the house to cast a cloud on a civil servant, whom he named, without someone coming to the defence of that civil servant. I do so very gladly because Mr. Driedger, who has been mentioned by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is a trusted servant of the crown and the opinions he gave when we were in office were opinions based on his belief and integrity-and I did not get the impression from the statement made by the Minister of Justice that Mr. Driedger gave an entirely different opinion to him.
I understood him to say there was doubt in the minds of some people, and for the removal of that doubt it might be wise to have a statute passed, such as is here before us; but I do take exception, and strong exception, to attacks on civil servants, and particularly on one who is a senior civil servant, a trusted civil servant, and who has no right of reply in this house.
I hope the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who delights in lecturing us from time to time as to our duties and responsibilities, will recognize his duty and responsibility in this connection. I have the greatest pleasure in lecturing a member of that party that sits on the sidelines so often and tells us what to do, and how the party that is now in office is acting just as the former government acted, and that both are wholly wrong. A party which has little hope of ever forming a government spends a lot of time telling the rest of us what to do.
My hon. friend is a fellow-citizen of that great city where I claim citizenship, and I think he has made a mistake in the course of his remarks today in his anxiety to protect the country against faults, as he sees them, that have perhaps occurred in the past.

However, a number of things have been said by members on both sides of this house, in this chamber and in other places in Canada, with which we simply do not agree.

We heard the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings say there was no difficulty in June respecting their interpretation of whether the surcharges were legal or not. We have heard, too, the Leader of the Opposition say, perhaps inside this house, but certainly outside, that he knew of no crisis in international exchange affairs until after June 18, 1962. I want to say that either this statement is not true or the right hon. gentleman was derelict in his duty. If he did not know there was a crisis in international exchange prior to June 18, then he certainly did not know what was going on in the economy of Canada. I wish to say that we think the action which was taken on June 24 in imposing these surcharges was taken too late. We also believe that this action was delayed until that date for reasons which were not in the best interest of the people of Canada. They may have been in the best interest of the Conservative party which was involved in an election, but certainly it was not for the good of the people of Canada that the government should have allowed our reserves to fall to such a dangerously low level before action was taken to halt the drain.
We have an obligation to validate these measures now, so that there may not be a possibility of some of the persons first charged with the payment of the tax receiving a windfall by way of refund, but we do not accept the argument that there was no crisis apparent until after the date of the election.

The house resumed from Friday, November 1, consideration in committee of Bill C-95 to amend the Income Tax Act-Mr. Gordon- Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.

On clause 16-Exemption of income from manufacturing or processing business in designated areas.

Last Friday afternoon we spoke on this clause and we brought forward an amendment as follows:
That section 71A (1) (b) be amended by adding: "except that the provisions of this section shall apply only where the municipality in which such taxpayer carries on business has requested the benefit hereof, and that municipalities receiving such benefits must not be closer to each other than 100 miles".
This amendment was the result of a concerted effort by a number of members on this side to remove the injustice which is rampant as a result of the indiscriminate naming of these designated areas. We believe the federal government should not usurp the authority vested in the provincial and municipal authorities. In other words, the provinces and the municipalities are the ones who best know the needs of local areas. The provincial government, on the advice of the municipalities, best knows whether and where a stimulant should be administered to these corporate bodies. We wish to get legislation which would spread out the benefits flowing to these areas and which would not work to the detriment of other areas in the region, so we proposed there should be a distance of 100 miles between any areas which might be designated. However, after careful perusal and consideration of the words in the proposed amendment appearing after the word "hereof", we find our suggestion is not as workable as we formerly believed it was. Therefore, with the permission of my seconder, the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary, and with the unanimous consent of the committee, I ask permission to withdraw this amendment. I may say we intend to replace it with another which I am sure will be acceptable to all hon. members.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the committee willing to consent to the withdrawal of this proposed amendment?

Agreed.
Amendment withdrawn.

Since the committee has given unanimous consent to the withdrawal of this amendment, I should like to present another on similar lines. But before reading the amendment I should like to bring to the attention of the committee as forcefully as I can the great danger, the pitfalls, the discrimination involved, and the impracticability of applying this piece of legislation in all parts of Canada.
This legislation is another example of 60 days of hasty decision. We find ourselves being asked to pass clause 16 of this legislation and I think we should pause and be very
Income Tax Act
careful before we pass it. I would ask the other parties to my left in the house to join with us in supporting the amendment which I propose to put before the house.
The list of designated areas was established by order in council. I wish that the minister without portfolio, who comes from Brantford, had asked one question of his cabinet colleagues at that time. If he had done so we would not now find ourselves faced with this problem which affects not only my area but the area of the hon. member for Renfrew North and other areas in Canada. If he had only asked the question, "how will this affect communities in the surrounding area", before the order in council was passed we would not find ourselves confronted with the problem that exists in the industrial area which includes Galt, Kitchener, Hespeler, Preston and Guelph.
This is a piece of legislation, Mr. Chairman, that will not work in a practical way. It was brought before the house by those academic thinkers on the treasury benches who had no conception of its practical application. I have taken the time of the house before to bring various points to the attention of the house to show that the legislation is not workable. I will simply list them now. First of all, it is discriminatory. The Minister of Industry says: Yes, it is discriminatory; that is what we want it to be. The hon. member for Northumberland says: Yes, it is discriminatory; that is what we want. That may be all right in certain areas but you cannot have discrimination where there are adjacent cities.
Another point I brought to the attention of the house was the criterion by which these places were designated. The criterion used is not a practical one. It is an academic criterion. The six summer months have been taken and this does not give a fair assessment.
I have given the reasons why in former speeches. If you are going to use unemployment figures you should take the whole 12 months of the year. This makes it practical and possible for all communities in Canada to qualify, and does not discriminate against those with high summer employment or low winter employment.
The third point I mentioned before was that the legislation encroaches upon provincial and municipal autonomy, something that we must guard against very zealously. The fourth point which I mentioned before was that it is contradictory. We have the Minister of Finance asking us in Bill No. C-95 to pass legislation that will impose a penalty on American subsidiaries in Canada. On the other hand, we have his counterpart, the Minister of Industry, offering $400,000 on a silver platter to an American firm to locate in Canada. This is

Income Tax Act
the situation. They are at cross-purposes. The legislation is contradictory.
The fifth point I mentioned was that the legislation was not being accepted by industrialists generally. This legislation has been dreamed up on the basis of academic thinking and I for one should like to see practical legislation.
What has the press throughout the country had to say about this matter? Surely we can place some importance on what the press has had to say. The latest comment brought to my attention is found on the first page of the Canada section of Time magazine of November 8. Under the main heading "The Realm" there is the subheading, "Depressed? Who, Us?" There is a picture of the main street of this thriving city of Brantford. The article reads in part as follows:
At one end of town, a $750,000 motel Is going up opposite a spanking new shopping plaza; at the other, a $1.5 million General Hospital residence and nursing school. Fortnight ago, in fact, Brantford became Canada's first city to go over the top in its united appeal campaign.
The whole article is worth reading for those on the government side. Here is a full page from the Kitchener-Waterloo Record. There are pictures of the Brantford employment office with no one in it, park benches with no one sitting on them and the busy main street, in fact, a town hustling and bustling with trade. I have here an article from the Globe and Mail of November 2 last which shows average earnings for Guelph of $4,232 and average earnings for Brantford of $4,215, a difference of only $17 per capita between the two cities. Yet Brantford is designated as a depressed area and the surrounding cities, particularly Guelph, are not.
Here is another heading in the Guelph Mercury:	"Don't Need Extra Help". The
reference is to a statement by the mayor of Kelowna. Here is an editorial that appeared in the Guelph Mercury of October 24 last headed, "Who Wants to be Depressed?" There is an interesting paragraph which reads as follows:
Industry minister Drury has got a tiger by the tail in this issue, and he may end up wishing that he had let the normal laws of supply and demand attract new industries to areas where they are best suited.
Again I say that the practical application of the law of supply and demand would have been much better than the application of academic thinking such as we find in this legislation. And so I could go on. Other protests and articles have been written. Here is one from the Guelph Mercury of October

16 last headed, "Wants 'March' on Ottawa", which reads in part as follows:
Alderman Donald Snider of Waterloo Tuesday suggested a march on Ottawa to protest federal plans for legislation giving special tax concessions to 11 areas and 115 municipalities in Ontario to the detriment of other areas. A "freedom train"-
Here is a headline from the Globe and Mail of October 9 last: "New Hamburg to Join Protest to Ottawa". These are but some of the newspaper articles that have appeared from time to time about this very unsatisfactory academic, theoretical piece of legislation that we are being asked to pass in the house this afternoon.
Before I conclude by moving an amendment to clause 16 I respectfully solicit the support of the parties to my left. I know that some of their members have the same problem in their areas. I would ask members on the government side to let their conscience be their guide with regard to this legislation. Very few of them have risen in their places to defend it. Why? Because they know it is wrong. That is why they have not stood up to defend it. Now here is a chance for them to support the amendment which I propose to put before the house.
The Prime Minister, in replying to a letter from the Guelph chamber of commerce, had this to say:
The difficulty is to apply this principle fairly.
Even the Prime Minister knows there will be difficulty in applying this fairly.
I am sure you will understand that any definition is bound to produce some difficult, borderline cases. It certainly was not and is not the government's wish to discriminate against a new industrial development in Guelph.
Inasmuch as the Prime Minister has said in his letter that it is not the wish of the government to discriminate, I ask for the support of this amendment by members on the government side. The amendment is along the lines that as members of parliament we should respect the rights of the municipalities and the provinces. We should respect the autonomy of these areas. This is what the amendment is based on-respect for the autonomy of these municipalities.
I mentioned earlier that not long ago the provincial government passed legislation prohibiting municipalities from outbidding one another in order to attract industries to their municipalities. Here we have the senior government stepping over the provincial government, ignoring them completely and saying to Brantford in this instance: You are a designated area. I do not know whether the Minister without Portfolio from Brantford was present, but he is a member of the cabinet and I wish he had asked his colleagues this one question: If we designate Brantford,

what will the surrounding communities think about this legislation. If he had done so we would not find ourselves in this position today. So, Mr. Chairman, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Lennox (Mr. Alkenbrack):
That paragraph 71A, subsection 1 (b) is amended by adding:
"except that the provisions of this section shall apply only where the municipality in which such taxpayer carries on business has requested the benefit hereof".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first of all I should like to thank the hon. member, if he included me-and I am not sure he did, although perhaps I am entitled to think he might have- in his reference to the academic thinkers on this side of the house. I have spent a fairly strenuous life, and all the while have been charged with being one of the practical people of this world. In the past, a lot of people have said it would have been better if I had spent more time in school. I thank the hon. member for the promotion.
Now, a lot has been said about this particular clause. I do not think anything is to be gained by a rehash of the arguments pro and con on the subject of trying to assist slow economic growth areas and trying to provide additional employment. As I have said, there are those who think these matters should be left to the ordinary forces of supply and demand. There are others, and they include most of the people in Europe, who think it is the duty and responsibility of the government to do something about areas of slow growth by trying to provide opportunities for the people living in those areas.
Then there is the argument, and I think this is perhaps the argument that the hon. member has concentrated upon, concerning the criteria that should be used in establishing these areas. It is significant, however, that in the amendment he has included a provision that a designated area would not be eligible for this assistance unless it were forced to come to the government, hat in hand, asking that this be done. I do not know, but I suppose you could make some kind of argument along this line. However, I suggest to the hon. member and to other members of this committee, that if we accept the principle that the federal government has a responsibility for trying to provide additional employment in areas of slow growth and relatively high unemployment, then the government should act accordingly.
Now, the criteria for the selection of areas have been based on the employment and unemployment record for summer months rather than the annual average in order to avoid undue emphasis on winter unemployment in areas where the main problem is of
Income Tax Act
a seasonal character. Under the established criteria, a national employment service area qualifies as a designated area provided:
(a)	It has been classified by the Department of Labour as a labour surplus area for one half or more of the summer months, May to October, during the past eight years; and it has experienced an employment increase of less than one half the national average over the same period; or
(b)	It has been classified by the Department of Labour as a labour surplus area for one third or more of the summer months, May to October, during the past eight years; and it has experienced an employment decrease over the same period; or
(c)	It has been classified by the Department of Labour as a labour surplus area for one half or more of the summer months, May to October, during the past three years; and it has experienced an employment decrease in each one of the past three years.
(d)	However, an area shall not be designated if the average monthly national employment service registration for the three months of May, June and July, expressed as a percentage of the total number of paid workers in the area,
(i)	Is less in the current year than in the preceding year and less in the preceding year than in the year preceding that year, and
(ii)	Is less in the current year than in the year preceding the preceding year by at least 45 per cent; and the area would not, if the three months of May, June and July in the current year were considered to be a single month, have been classified by the Department of Labour as a substantial labour surplus area for that month.
Provision is made for flexibility-and I do not believe enough has been said about this -in extending boundaries of designated areas and for adding new national employment service areas to the list of designated areas as soon as they fulfil the criteria of eligibility. All national employment service areas will be reviewed annually by the Department of Labour, and those new areas which qualify, along with those areas which no longer qualify, will be announced by that department.
The Minister of Industry, Mr. Chairman, has stated that the government intends to apply the various programs of assistance to industry in the designated areas as soon as possible. The area development agency will co-ordinate these activities for the government of Canada. Through the co-operative efforts of government and industry, economic activity will be stimulated in areas that have experienced slow growth and heavy unemployment for a long time. The Minister of

Income Tax Act
industry has stated that it this formula is found not to work in practice or to be susceptible of improvement, then he will be the first to recommend this improvement.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, to hon. members of the committee that the thing we should try to do now is get on with this particular measure for improving the rate of growth in certain areas of Canada and for providing more jobs in those areas, without further delay. I am afraid, Mr. Chairman, that I must say to the hon. member, on behalf of the members on this side of the house, we will be unable to accept his amendment.

Mr. Chairman, I want to make my remarks on this point very brief because the amendment that has been made would suggest to us further that, if only we had a government financial policy in Canada that was directed to our economic responsibility everywhere as it should be, we would not be talking about depressed areas and granting them special tax concessions. This clause with which we are dealing specifically is to provide a 36-month exemption from tax for new manufacturing or processing businesses being established in designated areas. The problem that is dealt with in this amendment is how the area shall be selected or designated as a depressed or needy area.
I am somewhat disappointed that the Minister of Finance has seen fit to reject this amendment, because I think it is aimed at a very fundamental problem of which we who are in the legislative business ought to be continually mindful. The clause provides that the Minister of Industry can designate an area. We have here more discretionary powers being put into the hands of government. It seems to me that government should want to have the advice and full co-operation of the communities with which they are concerned. The only way in which this can be accomplished is to take those communities into the confidence of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I wonder if the hon. member would allow me to ask him a question? The areas as defined are not confined to municipal boundaries, and I am just curious, since I gather he is supporting this amendment, to know how he thinks it would work in practice when it is intended to help areas that are not restricted to any particular municipal boundary limits?

I am quite aware of that. It was for this reason I was careful to use the word "communities", because in "communities" you might have several municipal or local governments. Certainly, you have the provincial government to which these local governments are responsible. How much more

effective it would be if these governments were consulted, if they were allowed to express their opinions on this.
I am in favour of this amendment for two reasons, and one is that the consultation aspect of government must be continually protected and preserved. It is only in this way we can get the full co-operation not only of local governments but also of people in industries and commercial enterprises in these communities. This applies even to the provincial governments because, after all, our municipalities are responsible to them.
From the second standpoint what I am particularly concerned about is that this bill is placing more discretionary powers in the hands of a central government, and this is the very thing we should be most concerned about as governments get larger and larger.
I would like to ask another question concerning something not touched by the amendment, but which is in a section preceding the amendment. Paragraph (a) states:
-occurring wholly within the 36 months period that commenced on the day certified as the day on which the business commenced manufacturing or processing in reasonable commercial quantities;
Just what would a "reasonable commercial quantity" be? It seems to me that paragraph (a) is very general and ambiguous, while the other is just the opposite, in that it is placing authority back into the hands of the minister.
I regret that the minister has taken the attitude he has just expressed because this is a very vital point, even though it is a minor one.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
I shall intervene only for a few minutes to support the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Wellington South. The basic idea of this legislation is, of course, to assist generally in the areas outlined by the government, but a very worthy point has been mentioned by the hon. member for Red Deer regarding the discretionary power of the Minister of Finance in determining who shall be eligible. To me this sounds like a peculiar way of approaching the question of how the areas are going to be designated.
Early this year, last year and the year before, one would have thought, listening to the minister's colleagues, that the whole of Canada was depressed; but now, as I said last week, we narrow it down to Liberal ridings. It seems, particularly with regard to the area that has been designated in Ontario, and which has caused a controversy, there must have been some particular pressure within the cabinet to designate that area. In fact it looks like a little bit of empire building around that particular city.
It only became evident to me after I had an opportunity of reading Hansard of last

week, when we were discussing this particular item, why this particular area should have this preference, when Brantford and every other city in the province of Ontario is enjoying prosperity as a result of the action we took when in office. There is no question about that.
Today we dealt with the surcharges and disposed of that particular measure. Some hon. members might think this is irrelevant, but I want to bring it to the attention of the committee to show that this particular method of dealing with the matter, such as the minister has proposed in the bill, is wrong, and that the hon. member for Wellington South might have the right idea here. At least it would be done on the basis of something that can be considered by an area which is anxious to take advantage of this legislation.
The surcharges, be they good, bad or indifferent, legal or illegal, were introduced and contributed immeasurably to the prosperity we are enjoying today. In fact I recall reading a letter in this chamber from a manufacturer making that very point, that they contributed to our prosperity, and therefore the government does not have to bring forward measures such as this to pinpoint certain areas and be discriminatory, as was stated by the minister's parliamentary secretary.
If all the municipalities in the Dominion of Canada are to have an advantage, surely it should be stated that way, and surely when an industry expands, and makes a contribution where unemployment has been a big factor, it should be for the benefit of the entire country and not limited to some place which the Minister of Finance says needs this assistance. That is not the philosophical thinking of the people on this side of the house. We think everybody should have the advantage and that that is the only fair way of dealing with the situation.
To conclude my brief remarks I say that if the minister really and truly wants to do something for the benefit of all the people of Canada and all the industries in Canada, he will remove the ridiculous sales tax imposition which is going to obstruct the expansion of industry. He might also do something about transportation so that areas, such as the area in which I live, can take advantage of it to attract industry.
