If the minister would do something of this nature that would affect all industries equally he would be contributing to the expansion of industry in all municipalities. We in my particular area would like to take advantage
Income Tax Act
of this, but we are experiencing the boom that the Conservative government instituted early in 1962. If the amendment presented by the hon. member for Wellington South were accepted, then I am sure representatives of the municipalities in my constituency would come down here and point out that they can use it to their advantage, and therefore to the advantage of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, the matter
of provincial autonomy was put forward, so to speak, when this amendment was introduced. After considering the amendment, I feel that it actually goes against the principles of provincial autonomy as we understand it. Municipalities spring from the provinces. If the federal government is to be allowed to deal directly with the municipalities, to override provincial governments, the central government will be inclined more and more to follow that course. It is precisely to that principle that we object.
On the other hand, if the hon. member who introduced this amendment would replace the word "municipality" by the word "province", then the amendment would be not only acceptable, but desirable. It would follow that the federal government would no longer have to deal with the municipalities but only with certain provincial governments. That would relieve the federal government of extra work, difficulties and problems. They would negotiate only with ten provincial governments, or at least with those interested, the province of Quebec being one of them. But the federal government is asked in this amendment to negotiate with every municipality.
Now, take my own riding, for instance, which is one of the designated areas-and my thanks to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon), to the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) and to the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) for having had the good idea of including the constituency of Lapointe among the designated areas. I say to those hon. ministers that they should have thought of that a long time ago, because in the constituency of Lapointe, the unemployed, the small industry and farmers have been in dire straits for quite some time.
That is because they have a bad member of parliament.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Chairman, I think it would be very easy to refute the charge just made by the hon. member for Dollard (Mr. Rouleau) and the hon. member for Mercier (Mr. Boulanger), for if our ridings are going through a period of distress, depression and unemployment, it is not the fault of the

Income Tax Act
members of the opposition, who have not even got their say in that, but the fault of the members of the party in office who have always refused to open their eyes and use their brains in order to accept the suggestions we have made to them in the past. It is because they turned a deaf ear to all our suggestions that they find themselves today without any solution to the problems facing us. Let the hon. member for Dollard and the hon. member for Mercier use their intelligence and stop being dense like all government members, and let them accept the solutions we are suggesting. They will realize then that the hon. member for Lapointe has the proper answers likely to solve the unemployment problem.
You never settled anything.

The hon. member for Dollard refuses to consider this solution with an open mind, like all other present government members and those of previous governments. That is why the appropriate solutions could never be found.
Mr. Chairman, there are other remarks I wanted to make to the Minister of Finance regarding this bill, namely this one which is worth considering, because I believe that the experts of the Department of Finance have succeeded in doing something that nobody could ever bring off in the whole world. I am referring to a sentence that I find in the French version of Bill No. C-95.
In fact, it begins at the bottom of page 14, and it continues on page 15 to end at the top of page 16; just one sentence with one semicolon only.
Mr. Chairman, I submit that it takes genius and these people must be outstanding to be able to compose one sentence extending nearly a page and a half.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not guilty.

I shall point out to the minister that really he could have experts with a different inclination, that is to make that piece of legislation clearer, less ambiguous and more concise.
It is true that there is a semicolon after the first 32 lines, but the period comes only after the next 30 lines, which means a sentence of 62 lines.
I noticed that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Favreau) was sitting next to the Minister of Finance a while ago, and seemed to be giving him advice. I have no doubt about the intellectual capacity of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, because I have always respected his talent for literature.

I notice also the presence of the Minister without Portfolio and President of the Privy Council (Mr. Lamontagne), who was a university professor.
I notice also the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chevrier), who is also a university graduate.
They are all good French Canadians who must strain their ingenuity, now and then in order to give the French language its inherent pungency and zest. And when I notice sentences like the one just mentioned which make up a page and a half, I am convinced that these three ministers will approve what I say.
I should have mentioned also the Postmaster General (Mr. Denis), but I will inquire about his linguistic qualifications and then I will be able to quote him once in a while.
Order.

At any rate, I submit that my remarks are in order, because when mentioning that clause, I am pointing out its defective terminology and punctuation or, rather, the inexact idea intimated therein, because it is impossible to express any idea clearly in a sentence a page and a half long.
I would also like to bring another point to the attention of the Minister of Finance. Everybody mentioned the designated areas which need help.
I had the opportunity of meeting some commission members, businessmen and municipal councillors in my riding, and to discuss matters with aldermen, mayors and reeves. Having done so, I realize that it is alright to exempt new industries from taxation, but in order to help administer the act appropriately the officials of the department of finance, or labour, and more particularly those in the employment office should be at the disposal of city councils, industrial commissions and municipalities, when they want advice, statistics and data, and all information required to help attract new industries to the various designated areas.
I think the employees of the various employment offices throughout the country, should be asked to supply our municipalities and industrial commissions with all statistical data that would help determine which industries might more particularly benefit by settling in one designated area rather than another. Then, being administered in practical way the law would become more efficient and benefit the designated areas to a greater extent.
That is why I would suggest to the Minister of Labour that he ask all his officials in employment and unemployment insurance offices to help, and co-operate with, as much

Business of the House
as possible, municipal councils and industrial commissions in order to give them the required information and statistics for the establishment of new industries in those various places called designated areas.
With respect to section 16, I should like to point out to the minister-and the Minister of Finance must be aware of that, since he was for several years an outstanding accountant working for an equally outstanding firm- that any company entering into business does not, in the first 12 months, or in many case in the first 24 months, and even in the first 36 months, make any profits and, therefore, would not benefit from a tax abatement.
I daresay to the minister that a new industry will show a deficit.
Then, those new industries coming into operation in the designated areas will suffer a loss, an operation deficit, and consequently they will not have to pay taxes. If that situation comes about for any normal industry, the same thing will affect an industry starting its operations, its marketing and its production in the designated areas.
So, the tax exemption granted to new industries for a three year period will not be beneficial to them if it is limited to three years. In certain cases, it will be six months, or a year, or even two years.
For those reasons, I am asking the Minister of Finance if he could not change a provision of the bill so that it would read as follows: for the first three years during which an industry would be paying taxes if it were taxable, that is if it showed operation surpluses subject to tax payments.
Then, there would be a true three year tax exemption benefit, while under the present legislation, an industry does not benefit from it for three years but for much shorter period if it happens that a new industry does not make any profits for the first two, three or even the first four years.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I see it is six o'clock. In any case-
Question.

Mr. Chairman, I see that the hon. members are in a hurry to vote. I am prepared to agree to their request, because on the same section, another member of our group will move an amendment. Then, I shall have the opportunity to give more advice to the Minister of Finance and I hope it will be followed.
The members who a few minutes ago blamed us for having depressed areas in our ridings suffer from a lack of intelligence, and I would suggest that they listen to the speeches dealing with unemployment in our constituencies.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Is the committee
ready for the question?

Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member for Lapointe did a very successful job in talking out the very worth while amendment put in by the hon. member for Wellington South. I see it is now six o'clock. Shall I proceed with my remarks, Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. It being six o'clock shall I rise, report progress, and request leave to sit again at the next sitting of the house?

Agreed.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the house would give unanimous consent to revert to motions purely for the purpose of substituting somebody on a committee.

subtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Agreed.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I move, seconded by the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret):
That the name of Mr. Olson be substituted for that of Mr. Girouard on the standing committee on privileges and elections.

subtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words on that motion.

subtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: No.

subtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to point out that on the privileges and elections committee we, of the Ralliement Creditistes, have only one representative, while the group of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) has two. The same thing prevails in every one of the special or standing committees of the house.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Order. I must bring to the attention of the hon. member that the motion moved by the hon. member is not open to debate.
I am sorry; I have just been told that the motion is open to debate, but only on changes brought about in particular circumstances.

subtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is precisely what I have in mind; I am dealing with such changes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the said motion?

subtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is precisely on the point we have just referred to and

Business of the House
which directly concerns the change that I should like to propose an amendment to the motion.
I have made my preliminary statement and I feel the arguments I am using are permissible in the course of the debate on the motion.
As I was saying, the membership of the standing and special committees of the house is not fairly divided among each party, especially as far as the Ralliement Creditistes is concerned. For instance, on the defence committee-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Order. In my opinion, the hon. member is wandering quite a bit from the subject of the motion now before us, and if I may read it in English-

That the name of Mr. Olson be substituted for that of Mr. Girouard on the standing committee on privileges and elections.
That is the only thing which can be discussed by the hon. member because that is the only motion before the house at the moment.

subtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is precisely what I wish to discuss, and to come to the point, in view of the poor distribution-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CHANGE IN PERSONNEL OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Order. I must point out to the hon. member that his remarks are not relevant to the motion before the house.
Perhaps, he could wait for another opportunity to make them.
Motion agreed to.
May I inquire from the Secretary of State what the business of the house will be for tomorrow, and also for Friday as well.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Tomorrow we will continue with the committee stage, and I hope also the third reading of the bill under consideration a few minutes ago, the income tax bill. Under the agreement I mentioned last night, when it is completed we will take, up until five o'clock, the motion in the name of my hon. friend the Solicitor General, which everyone is anxious to reach. If that is completed I should like to call second reading of the Northwest Territories Act once more.
Will the same order be followed on Friday?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.
It being five minutes past six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put.
